strengths: Addresses a highly relevant and growing bottleneck in LLM deployment: the serving efficiency and scheduling of tool-augmented or agentic LLMs.

Proposes a solid, well-formulated two-stage scheduling strategy that combines offline prediction (Stage I) with online runtime correction (Stage II) to handle the uncertainty of external API call durations and response lengths.
Introduces a dynamic token-level batching mechanism that effectively leverages available GPU memory and accounts for paused requests' context, avoiding conservative static limits.

Provides extensive evaluations across multiple distinct hardware setups (NVIDIA RTX 4090, H800, A100) and realistic workloads (Poisson, Gamma, bursty traffic), showing significant gains in goodput and reduction in tail latencies.
weaknesses: The system relies on a BERT-base-uncased predictor for initial estimation. Though the paper shows low time overhead (< 1%), the memory footprint and concurrent execution overhead of running an auxiliary BERT model on memory-constrained consumer GPUs (like the RTX 4090) are not thoroughly analyzed.

The impact of predictor error on the scheduler's behavior is not deeply studied. For instance, the output length prediction accuracy is only 65% on the Merge dataset; a systematic analysis of how the system performs under worst-case prediction errors before Stage II corrects them would strengthen the paper.

While equations 23-25 mention multi-round/cross-round considerations, the evaluation does not explicitly detail or benchmark complex multi-turn/multi-hop agent scenarios where sequential tool calls occur repeatedly in a single session.

strengths: Addresses a highly relevant and growing challenge in LLM serving: optimizing scheduling and throughput for tool-augmented large language models (agents) which feature complex pause/resume states and uncertain external tool outputs.
Provides a well-motivated, two-stage adaptive request scheduling strategy that elegantly balances predictive estimation (Stage I) with runtime correction (Stage II) and anti-starvation mechanisms.
A dynamic token-level batching mechanism is proposed to adapt to real-time workloads and GPU memory conditions, replacing rigid static limits.

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (Merge, ToolBench), models (GPT-J-6B, OPT-13B), and diverse GPU hardware (4090, H800, A100) showing substantial improvements in goodput, TTFT, and normalized latency over state-of-the-art baselines like vLLM and InferCept.
weaknesses: The paper lacks detail on the practical deployment overhead of the prediction module (BERT-base-uncased). Hosting a secondary model alongside the LLM consumes GPU/CPU resources and memory; a brief discussion on where this model runs (CPU vs. GPU) and its memory footprint is missing.

The sensitivity of the Stage I scheduler to prediction inaccuracies is not fully explored. While Stage II acts as a corrective measure, the impact of the BERT predictor's accuracy (which is 65% on the Merge dataset) on the initial queuing delay should be evaluated.

The physical intuition behind some of the cost formulations in Section 4.3 (such as the quadratic relationships in Eq. 9, 10, 12) is not explicitly explained, which might make it difficult for readers without a deep systems background to follow the mathematical models.

strengths: Practical and timely topic: Optimizing the inference serving of tool-augmented LLMs is highly relevant given the growing deployment of LLM agents and function-calling services.

Adaptive two-stage design: Combining prediction-driven scheduling (Stage I) with runtime-driven corrections (Stage II) is a robust and elegant way to mitigate the inherent uncertainty of tool-call durations and return lengths.

Extensive evaluation: The paper validates the system under diverse hardware configurations (RTX 4090, H800, A100), varying workloads (Poisson, Gamma, fixed requests), and multiple model sizes, showing clear throughput and latency improvements over vLLM and InferCept.
Detailed and thorough system description: The paper provides clear mathematical formulations for estimating phase costs and includes a complete, concrete scheduler algorithm in the appendix.
weaknesses: Dependency on prediction accuracy: The scheduling performance is tied to a BERT-base model whose classification accuracy on output length prediction is relatively low (65% on the Merge dataset). A detailed sensitivity analysis is lacking to show how robust the system is to high prediction errors or out-of-domain workloads.

Prediction overhead: While the paper states that prediction accounts for less than 1% of total request time, the absolute latency and memory footprint of running the BERT model's forward pass should be quantified, particularly on memory-constrained consumer GPUs like the RTX 4090.

Heuristic complexity and generalization: The scheduling strategy relies on numerous mathematical formulations (Equations 4-26) with many profiling parameters (e.g., swap-in/out speeds, forward time). This high parameterization may make the system difficult to tune and generalize to heterogeneous or cloud environments without extensive offline profiling.

Limited scheduling baselines: While InferCept is an appropriate state-of-the-art baseline, the paper would benefit from comparing against other general scheduling strategies (such as FastServe or S3) adapted to tool-augmented workloads to isolate the scheduling benefits from the context-handling policies.

strengths: Highly relevant and timely problem: addressing inference scheduling and memory management for tool-augmented large language models (LLMs) which exhibit heterogeneous and unpredictable execution states.

Principled system design: the proposed space-time cost model (integrating memory footprint over residency time) and the feedback-driven post-invocation refinement offer a robust way to handle estimation errors in external call latencies.
Dynamic token budget mechanism: incorporating reclaimable memory from paused requests under different context-handling policies (Swap/Discard) allows the system to maximize concurrency and goodput.

Extensive and thorough evaluation: the authors evaluate AugServe across multiple hardware platforms (4090, H800, multi-A100), diverse LLM sizes (up to Llama-3-70B), and multiple baselines (including vLLM, INFERCEPT, and MARS).
weaknesses: Although the prediction model (BERT-base, 110M) is claimed to run off the critical path, invoking it on every request arrival and tool return may introduce non-trivial CPU/GPU resource contention and latency overhead under ultra-high-throughput settings.

The system relies on multiple hyperparameters (such as beta, beta_low, beta_high, and the reference offline budget Tmax). While a sensitivity study is provided for beta, the guidelines or sensitivity for tuning the other bounds and scaling factors under highly dynamic workloads remain less explored.

The 1/2-approximation guarantee provided in Theorem E.1 is limited to a highly simplified, static 0-1 knapsack subproblem for a single iteration, leaving a gap between the theoretical guarantees and the actual online, multi-stage dynamic scheduling execution.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated identification of the limitations of existing LLM serving frameworks (like vLLM and INFERCEPT) under augmented LLM workloads with external calls.
Comprehensive and cohesive system design combining lightweight prediction, state-aware space-time cost modeling, feedback-driven priority refinement, and dynamic batch-level token budgeting.

Extensive evaluation spanning multiple GPU architectures (RTX 4090, H800, A100), diverse LLM sizes (6B to 70B), and realistic arrival workloads, demonstrating major improvements in both goodput and latency metrics (TTFT, normalized latency).
Thorough ablation and sensitivity studies, demonstrating the robustness of the scheduler to prediction errors and analyzing the overhead of the scheduling algorithm.
weaknesses: Deploying an external 110M BERT-base model for prediction increases operational complexity and memory footprint on serving nodes, which might be a bottleneck in resource-constrained environments.

The 1/2-approximation theoretical guarantee only applies to a highly simplified, single-iteration knapsack subproblem, failing to capture the full complexity of the online multi-stage scheduling problem.

The performance of the predictive initialization relies on fine-tuning on specific datasets (ToolBench/INFERCEPT). Its generalizability and robustness to completely unseen, out-of-distribution external APIs are not fully explored.

strengths: The paper targets a highly relevant and timely problem: optimizing the inference serving of augmented LLMs (agentic workflows invoking external APIs/tools).
The proposed framework, AugServe, jointly optimizes request scheduling and batch-level token budget adaptation, directly addressing the key limitations of existing work (such as INFERCEPT and vLLM).
The state-aware space-time cost model and the post-invocation refinement strategy are well-designed, offering a elegant way to integrate feedback and handle prediction inaccuracies.

The evaluation is exceptionally thorough, spanning multiple models (including Llama-3-70B), multiple GPU platforms (RTX 4090, H800, A100), diverse datasets (ToolBench, INFERCEPT), and showcasing significant goodput and latency improvements.
Excellent presentation, with clear diagrams, comprehensive mathematical formulations, and detailed ablation studies.
weaknesses: The system relies on a fine-tuned 110M BERT predictor to estimate output lengths and external call durations. While the authors demonstrate robustness to prediction errors, training and deploying this extra model introduces cold-start overhead and operational complexity when transitioning to new datasets/workloads.

The theoretical approximation analysis in Appendix E is limited to a simplified, static, single-iteration knapsack model, which does not capture the complex online, multi-round scheduling dynamics of the actual system.

The paper primarily assumes sequential segment-level execution. It is not fully clear how the framework handles more complex agentic patterns, such as nested tool calls, parallel tool execution, or dynamic branching during tool-use.
